## Routing

**Triggers:** learn, remember, "we always", "last time", memory, instinct, "what did we decide".
**USE FOR:** capturing a durable lesson, promoting a repo instinct to shared memory,
querying what is already known.
**NOT FOR:** recording an architecture decision — that is `architecture-decision`.
Client requirements — that is `knowledge-base`.

## The Tiers

| Tier | Path | Scope | Synced |
|------|------|-------|--------|
| Shared | `memory/shared/` | All repos | Yes |
| Per-repo | `memory/repos/<name>/` | One repo | Only that repo |
| Decisions | `memory/decisions/<slug>.jsonl` | One repo, append-only | No — promote explicitly |
| Session | `memory/sessions/` | One pipeline run | No, git-ignored |

## The Promotion Rule, And The Gate After It

An entry becomes a **candidate** for shared memory when **confidence ≥ 0.7 AND it has
been observed in ≥ 2 repos.** Both conditions, not either.

A high-confidence lesson from a single repository is usually a fact about that
repository, not a general truth. Promoting it early is exactly how a shared memory fills
with advice that is wrong everywhere else — and shared memory is loaded into every
session in every repo, so a wrong entry is expensive in a way a wrong comment is not.

**Meeting the criteria does not promote anything.** The lifecycle is:

```
candidate ──criteria met──> pending-approval ──human──> approved ──> retired
                                             └─human──> rejected (durable)
```

Confidence and repo-count measure how OFTEN something was observed. They do not measure
whether it is TRUE, and no arithmetic over observation counts ever will. A human names an
entry as organizational guidance before it becomes organizational guidance:

```
python scripts/memory.py promote            # propose candidates, write review artifacts
python scripts/memory.py pending            # what is awaiting a decision
python scripts/memory.py approve <id> --by "<name>"
python scripts/memory.py reject  <id> --reason "..."
python scripts/memory.py retire  <id> --reason "..."
```

Rejection is durable, deliberately: without it a rejected entry keeps meeting the
criteria and gets re-proposed on every run, which teaches the reviewer to stop reading.
Retirement keeps the entry rather than deleting it — what the organization believed, and
when it stopped believing it, is part of the record.

The test to apply when approving: *would you write this on the team wiki as guidance for
every project?* If not, reject it and say why.

## The Confidence Arithmetic

Confidence is not a feeling; something computes it:

```
initial:  0.4    one observation, one repo — deliberately below the 0.7 floor, so no
                 single event can promote anything no matter how sure the agent felt
+0.15            reinforced in a NEW repo          ← the primary path to promotion
+0.05            reinforced in a repo already seen
-0.25            a counter-example was recorded
-0.05 / 90 days  decay since lastReinforced, applied lazily at READ time
clamp(0.1, 0.95)
```

Decay is **for ranking, never for deletion.** Deletion-by-decay stays deferred because
calibrating a rate needs real usage data and a wrong rate would silently discard useful
learnings. Ranking decay discards nothing — it only stops a three-year-old instinct from
outranking last week's — so a wrong rate there is cheap and correctable.

## Deduplicate Before You Append

Compare on **title and resolution, never on context.** Context is repo-specific and
differs even when the lesson is word-for-word identical, so comparing it guarantees you
never detect a duplicate. A strong match reinforces the existing entry instead of
appending; that reinforcement is what moves confidence toward the promotion floor.

## Every Write Is Guarded

`scripts/memory.py` is the only supported write path, and it runs the redaction and
injection scan first. There is no flag that skips it.

Two reasons, and the second is the less obvious one. Shared memory syncs
organization-wide, so a captured credential is a replication event rather than a local
mistake. And stored memory is re-injected into future prompts, which makes the memory
store an **injection surface** as well as a storage surface — a "resolution" that says
"ignore previous instructions" is a delayed instruction, read back to an agent in three
months, in a different repo, with no human in the loop.

## Commands

```
python scripts/memory.py capture --type anti-pattern --title "..." --resolution "..."
python scripts/memory.py search "<query>"
python scripts/memory.py promote            # apply the promotion rule
python scripts/memory.py prune              # interactive; below 0.3 and cold 180 days
```

## Grounding Contract

Cite `file:line` for every claim about this codebase. A claim you cannot cite is not a
finding — it is a guess wearing a finding's clothes.

- If a file or symbol is not in the evidence manifest, either open it and cite what you
  find, or say it was not found. An honest "not found" outranks a plausible guess.
- **Negative claims need evidence too.** "There is no handler for X" is a claim about
  the codebase and carries the same burden as "X is handled in Y". Unsupported absence
  assertions are as wrong as unsupported presence assertions, and they get challenged
  far less often.
- Never continue past a `_[truncated by token budget]_` marker as if you had read the
  remainder. Ask for the rest of the file.
- Never describe code you have not read in this session. Recalling a pattern from
  training and reading a file are different acts, and only one of them is evidence.

## Output Contract

State what you produced, where it landed, and what you deliberately did not do.

- Name every file you created or modified, with its path.
- Separate what you **verified** from what you **believe**. Use the confidence markers.
- Close with **Deliberately skipped** — the things in scope that you chose not to do,
  and why. An omission the reader has to discover is a defect; an omission you name is
  a decision.
- If a step could not run, report it as "not run" with the reason. Never report an
  unrun step as passed, and never report an unrun step as failed.

## Lessons Learned

_Empty at ship. The `continuous-learning` skill appends here; this is how a skill
self-evolves. Entries are added by `python scripts/memory.py promote`, never by hand
during a task — a lesson written mid-task is usually a fact about that task._
